newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan markets sink on remarks by "Mr Yen".
newsitem.headline: Japan markets sink on remarks by "Mr Yen".

text.p: The dollar tumbled, stocks fell sharply and Japanese government bonds were sold off on Thursday after one of Japan's most influential financial policymakers signalled that the long slide in the yen had gone far enough.

Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr Yen" for his role in taming the raging yen last year, was quoted as saying in a newspaper that the dollar's recovery from its sharp slide last year was about to finish. The dollar has risen 40 percent since hitting a post-war low of 79.75 yen in April 1995.

Sales intensified later when Sakakibara, director general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, in remarks to Reuters, backed up the statements and added fuel to the fire by saying that the Japanese economy was stronger than the markets believed.
He said the ministry was closely watching the foreign exchange markets, where the dollar has sharply strengthened recently, but declined comment on specific currency rates or the article.
The dollar fell quickly from a morning high of 113.80 yen to a low of 112.01 yen on aggressive sales spearheaded by overseas operators.

"Including today, comments from the Japanese side had been voicing caution towards a higher dollar. But on the other hand, U.S. officials have stuck to their policy of seeking a strong dollar. There seems to be a gap between Japanese and U.S. officials," said Takashi Itoda, manager of the international planning department at Dai-ichi Mutual Life Insurance.
The dollar recovered some ground to trade here at 112.30 yen in late activity, helped by vague market rumours of Bank of Japan dollar buying in the market.
Tokyo stocks fell sharply on the higher yen, reversing gains made before the currency started its fall.
The key 225-share Nikkei average slipped 220.41 points or 1.05 percent to finish at 20,771.11.

"A continued yen weakening would have encouraged the outlook on Japanese corporate earnings, but such a rise hurts the prospects of foreign investor buying," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.

Japanese government bonds (JGBs), already under selling pressure for the second consecutive day, were hit with intensive selling after Sakakibara said the market view on the economy was too pessimistic.
The fall in price pushed up the yield on the benchmark 10-year bond to 2.6 percent from 2.5 percent at Wednesday's close.
The greenback's steep decline also led to sharp drops across the board in U.S. Treasury bonds, which were put under heavy selling pressure from the start of trade.

"The dollar's fall was the key factor that triggered heavy sales today," a senior trader at a major brokerage house said. "Strong sales came from overseas in the futures market weighed heavily on cash prices."
The benchmark 30-year bond fell to 101-5/32 in Tokyo, down 18/21 from the New York close on Wednesday. It later rebounded slightly to 101-7/32.
